definitions.meaning: The smallest particle of an element that keeps its chemical identity: a tiny dense nucleus with electrons in shells around mostly empty space.
The tiny dense centre of the atom, holding the protons and neutrons. Almost all the atom's mass sits here.
A particle in the nucleus with charge +1 and mass 1. The number of protons - the proton number - fixes which element the atom is.
A particle in the nucleus with no charge and mass 1. Neutrons = nucleon number - proton number.
A particle with charge -1 and almost no mass, sitting in fixed shells around the nucleus. A neutral atom has equal electrons and protons.
A fixed energy level around the nucleus where electrons sit. Shells fill in order: shell 1 holds 2, shell 2 holds 8, shell 3 holds 8.
A column of the periodic table. Elements in one group share the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways.
A row of the periodic table. The period number matches the number of electron shells the atoms have.

mechanismSteps: Inside the atom - shells draw themselves around a tiny dense nucleus that grows at the centre, electrons drop into shell 1, and the space between stays empty: the atom is mostly empty space.
Counting particles: carbon - carbon is element 6, so six protons in the nucleus and six electrons around it fill the shells two, then four: 2,4.
Counting particles: sodium - sodium is element 11 with eleven protons, twelve neutrons and eleven electrons arranged 2,8,1, and the lone outer electron rules its chemistry.
Groups: the table's columns - a group shares the same number of outer electrons down the column, so its elements react in similar ways.
Periods: the table's rows - the period number matches the number of electron shells: period 2 has two shells, period 3 has three.
A common mistake - the ball-and-stick model makes atoms look like solid marbles, but the nucleus is a speck in the middle of empty space and electrons sit in fixed shells.
objectives: Describe the atom: a tiny dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells around mostly empty space
Count protons, neutrons and electrons from the proton and nucleon numbers
Use the electron arrangement to state an element's group and period
subject: science
title: Atomic structure and the periodic table

trap.explanation: The slip: The ball-and-stick model is everywhere, so atoms look like tiny solid marbles. The fix: Atoms are mostly empty space: the electrons sit far from a tiny dense nucleus. In class, compare the two pictures side by side: the solid marble, then the shell model with its speck of a nucleus - and ask which one explains why alpha particles mostly passed straight through gold foil.

workedExample: Read sodium off the table step by step. Step 1 (s3): sodium has proton number 11 and nucleon number 23, so it has 11 protons and 23 - 11 = 12 neutrons, and a neutral atom has 11 electrons. Step 2 (s3): the electrons fill the shells in order - 2 in shell 1, 8 in shell 2, and the last 1 in shell 3 - giving the arrangement 2,8,1. Step 3 (s4 and s5): three shells means period 3, and 1 outer electron means group 1. Check against carbon (s2): 6 protons, 6 neutrons, 6 electrons, arrangement 2,4 - two shells (period 2) and 4 outer electrons (group 4).
